doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Idris Muhammad's different beat
summary: He found Muhammad in New Orleans and credits his drumming for the hit sound.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Working with Idris Muhammad put a completely different framework on what you were doing.
He’s a great drummer. Great drummer.
Did he come as kind of a package deal with George Benson and Lonnie Smith?
No-no. I saw him down in New Orleans, and I got him from there. He was down there. I got him from down there. He’s a great drummer. Great beat.
it was a somewhat different beat than you’d been working with.
Can you talk about that a bit?

I don’t know what to talk about. It was just a different beat. He used to, like, ruffle on the drums, RRRPPP, DUH-DUHT-DUH-DUHT, RRRPPP. He had a different thing, that he was sliding on the drums. Other drummers hadn’t picked that up, and that was a big hit.
Those beats in still in common parlance. They’re being sampled...
Yeah, but they don’t sound like him. Unfortunately.

I’m asking about these sides because they’re still resonating with deejays, samples, in popular music... As you were describing earlier, though perhaps not this piece, Madonna had sampled a beat from one your sides, and you got a big check; Mary J. Blige has used these beats; and so on... Which is why I’m interested in what you were thinking about then in modifying your group sound in the latter part of the ‘60s?
It wasn’t no special effect. It was just that we were playing, and everybody played well together. That’s what made it sound like that.
So it had to do with everyone expressing their personalities on their instruments...
